title: What is an ICUMSA sugar grade?
excerpt: ICUMSA grades describe the colour of refined cane sugar. Lower numbers mean a whiter crystal — the number buyers use when specifying export sugar.
metaTitle: What is an ICUMSA sugar grade?
metaDescription: ICUMSA is a colour scale for sugar. Learn what ICUMSA 45, 100-150, and higher grades mean for wholesale buyers importing refined sugar from Thailand.
paragraphs: ICUMSA is the International Commission for Uniform Methods of Sugar Analysis. In wholesale trade, buyers almost always use “ICUMSA” as a colour grade: the number is a laboratory colour value. A lower number means a whiter, more highly refined crystal.

The scale exists so a mill in Thailand and a food plant in another country can specify the same product. A purchase contract that says “ICUMSA 45” is asking for a highly refined white sugar, not a brown or raw crystal.
ICUMSA 45 is the grade most often requested by beverage, confectionery, and industrial food manufacturers. It is among the whitest commercial cane sugars offered for export.
ICUMSA 100-150 is still refined sugar, but the colour value is higher, so the crystal is less brilliant white. Some specifications call for this range when a slightly warmer appearance is acceptable.

Higher numbers (for example 600-1,200 or 1,500-2,500) describe less fully refined or darker sugars used in industrial or specific process applications. They are not substitutes for ICUMSA 45 in a white-sugar recipe.
Colour is only one specification. Contracts should also cover moisture, grain size, packing, and documents. Colour grade does not by itself define polarity, ash, or microbiological limits.
When you request a quote from a Thai exporter, state the ICUMSA range, monthly or shipment volume, destination port, packaging, and Incoterm. That combination is what a mill or trader can price.

title: ICUMSA 45 vs ICUMSA 100-150: which sugar grade to specify?
excerpt: ICUMSA 45 is the whiter, more fully refined export grade. ICUMSA 100-150 is still refined sugar with a higher colour value. Choose from the specification, not from a retail label.
metaDescription: Compare ICUMSA 45 and ICUMSA 100-150 for wholesale buyers: colour, typical uses, and how to specify Thai refined sugar on an export contract.
paragraphs: Buyers comparing ICUMSA 45 and ICUMSA 100-150 are usually choosing how white the crystal must be. Both are refined cane sugars. They are not raw sugar, and they are not interchangeable with brown sugar.
ICUMSA 45 sits at the low (whiter) end of the colour scale. Food and beverage plants that need a bright white appearance in drinks, fondants, or light-coloured baked goods typically specify 45.

ICUMSA 100-150 has a higher colour number. The crystal can appear slightly less brilliant. It may fit processes where colour is less critical, or where the buyer’s existing specification already names that range.
Do not choose a grade only because one listing looks cheaper in a broker message. Price moves with volume, freight, packing, and timing. The wrong colour grade creates rejection risk at destination.

Ask the supplier to confirm the test method and the certificate that will accompany the shipment. Colour should be measured against the method named in the contract, not described only as “white” or “refined”.

If you are replacing an existing supplier, match the grade on your last accepted shipment first. Changing from 45 to 100-150 (or the reverse) can change dissolution appearance and finished-product colour.
UFI lists both ICUMSA 45 and ICUMSA 100-150 in the wholesale catalogue. Request a quote with destination, volume, and packing so sales can confirm availability against your specification.

title: How to import refined sugar from Thailand
excerpt: Importing Thai refined sugar is a specification, logistics, and document process: grade, volume, Incoterms, packing, and customs paperwork — not a retail checkout.
metaTitle: How to import refined sugar from Thailand
metaDescription: A practical path for importers: specify ICUMSA grade, agree Incoterms, pack for containers, and clear documents when buying wholesale refined sugar from Thailand.
paragraphs: Thailand is a major cane-sugar origin. Importers buy refined white and related grades for food manufacturing, distribution, and further processing. The work is contractual, not cart-based.
Start with a written specification: ICUMSA grade (or other colour/purity range), grain, packing (50 kg bags or jumbo bags), and the quantity per shipment or per month.
Agree the Incoterm. FOB and CIF are common on sugar parcels. The term decides who books freight and insurance and where risk transfers. Name the load port and destination port in the same discussion.
Ask for a commercial offer against that specification, not a website price. Export sugar is quoted for a quantity, packing, and shipment window.

Confirm documents before the vessel sails: commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, certificate of origin, and quality documents as the contract requires. Missing papers delay discharge more often than the sugar itself.
Check destination rules: import licences, tariff codes, and any local food-control registration. Those are the buyer’s responsibility in most Incoterms and vary by country.
Inspect packing photos or a packing list against the contract. Container stuffing, bag marks, and lot numbers should match what customs and your warehouse expect.

title: Wholesale sugar packaging and typical export quantities
excerpt: Export refined sugar is usually packed in 50 kg bags or jumbo bags and sold by the container or metric ton — not by the kitchen sack.
metaDescription: How Thai export sugar is packed (50 kg bags, jumbo bags) and how buyers should describe quantity and MOQ on a wholesale RFQ.
paragraphs: Retail sugar bags are not how export parcels move. Wholesale refined sugar from Thailand is packed for container transport and industrial receiving.
The most common retail-adjacent export pack is the 50 kg polypropylene bag, palletised or stuffed according to the contract. Marks on the bag should identify product, origin, and lot as agreed.
Jumbo bags (FIBCs) are used when the receiver can handle bulk bags, often 1,000 kg class. They reduce bag count but need the right forklift and discharge equipment.

Minimum order quantity is a commercial term, not a laboratory grade. Exporters usually think in metric tons or full containers. State your target quantity in tons and whether you can take a full container.
Do not leave packing implied. A quote for “sugar” without bag size, liner, and stuffing method is incomplete. Damage and shortage claims often start with unclear packing.
Moisture protection matters in tropical load ports. Contracts should say how bags are protected inside the container and whether desiccant or lining is required.
When you enquire with UFI, include packing preference, monthly or shipment tons, and destination. Sales can then align mill packing with your warehouse.

title: How quality is specified for Thai refined sugar exports
excerpt: Export quality is a written specification — ICUMSA colour, packing, and certificates — checked through refining and documents, not a marketing adjective.
metaDescription: How buyers should specify and verify quality on Thai refined sugar exports: ICUMSA grade, mill process, packing, and shipment documents.
paragraphs: “Premium” is not a test result. Buyers protect themselves by naming a grade, a method, and the documents that will prove it at load.
ICUMSA colour is the language most used for white refined cane sugar. Pair it with any other limits your plant requires (moisture, grain, insolubles) so the mill is not guessing.
Refining after raw sugar production is what produces a white crystal. The manufacturing process page outlines cultivation through crystallisation, refining, drying, and packing in general terms.
Quality control continues at packing: bag integrity, net weight, marks, and lot identity. A correct certificate attached to the wrong lot is still a failure.
Shipment documents should match the contracted specification. If the contract says ICUMSA 45, the quality document should not describe an unnamed “white sugar”.
Keep a retain sample policy if your inbound QC lab needs it. Agree sampling in the contract when destination testing will decide acceptance.
UFI’s quality standard page describes our commitment from process to shipment. Combine it with a product-page enquiry so the grade you want is the grade we quote.
If a term is unclear, use the glossary. ICUMSA, polarity, and Incoterms are defined there for buyers who are new to sugar contracts.

title: ICUMSA 45 sugar for food and beverage manufacturers
excerpt: ICUMSA 45 is the white refined grade most often specified by industrial users who need a consistent crystal for drinks, confectionery, and bakery.
metaDescription: Why food and beverage plants specify ICUMSA 45, what to put on the RFQ, and how UFI supplies this Thai refined white sugar grade for export.
paragraphs: Food and beverage manufacturers specify ICUMSA 45 when they need a highly refined white cane sugar that will not add unwanted colour to a light product.
Typical users include soft-drink bottlers, confectioners, dairy and bakery plants, and ingredient blenders who already have an ICUMSA 45 line on their raw-material list.
The grade is a colour target, not a recipe. Your process still needs the correct grain size, dissolving behaviour, and packing that your silo or bag dump can handle.
Write the RFQ like a materials specification: ICUMSA 45, quantity per month or per container, 50 kg or jumbo packing, destination port, and Incoterm. Add any extra limits your QA team requires.
Do not substitute a higher ICUMSA number without a plant trial. A darker crystal can shift beverage colour or fondant appearance even when sweetness is similar.
Lead time depends on mill production, packing, and vessel space. Give a target shipment month, not only “ASAP”, so the exporter can plan against real availability.
